title: Flow of Liquid in Capillary Tube
short_intro: The flow of liquid through a narrow cylindrical tube, or capillary tube, is governed by viscous forces under a pressure gradient. It is fundamentally described by Poiseuille's equation for streamlined, laminar flow.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of capillary rise, Jurin's law, factors affecting surface tension, and basic dimensional analysis of viscous flow.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of Poiseuille's formula, series and parallel combination of capillary tubes, end corrections, and kinetic energy corrections.

prerequisites: Bernoulli's theorem and equation of continuity

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Flow in Capillary Tubes
bullets: The flow of an incompressible Newtonian liquid through a long narrow tube of uniform circular cross-section is streamline or laminar.
Fluid velocity is maximum at the axis of the tube and drops to zero at the inner walls due to the no-slip condition.
The velocity profile across the cross-section of the capillary tube is parabolic in shape.

concept_notes.heading: Poiseuille's Law of Liquid Flow
bullets: The volume of liquid flowing per second (rate of flow, Q) through a capillary tube depends on the pressure gradient per unit length, radius of the tube, and coefficient of viscosity of the liquid.
Q is directly proportional to the fourth power of the radius (r<sup>4</sup>) and the pressure difference (P), and inversely proportional to the length of the tube (l) and viscosity (&eta;).
It applies strictly to steady, laminar flow without turbulence or turbulent kinetic energy losses.

concept_notes.heading: Capillary Combinations
bullets: When capillary tubes are joined in series, the rate of flow through each tube is the same, and the total pressure difference is the sum of pressure drops across individual tubes.
When capillary tubes are joined in parallel, the pressure difference across each tube is the same, and the total rate of flow is the sum of rates through individual tubes.
Equivalent viscous resistance for series combination is R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>, analogous to electrical resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Correction Factors in Capillary Flow
bullets: Hagen-Poiseuille formula assumes zero velocity at the entry and exit, which is idealized.
Traverse kinetic energy requires a correction term known as Hagenbach's correction, modifying the effective pressure head.
End corrections account for the constriction of streamlines just before entering the capillary tube.

derivations.title: Derivation of Poiseuille's Equation
derivations.conditions: Steady, laminar, streamline flow of a Newtonian fluid through a cylindrical tube of radius R and length l under pressure difference P.
steps: Consider a coaxial cylindrical fluid shell of inner radius x and thickness dx moving with velocity v. The viscous drag force acting on the outer surface of this shell is given by F = - &eta; (2&pi;x l) (dv/dx).

This viscous force is balanced by the net pressure force acting on the cross-section of the shell, which is F<sub>p</sub> = (P / l) (&pi;x<sup>2</sup>). Equating the two forces gives -&eta;(2&pi;xl)(dv/dx) = (P/l)(&pi;x<sup>2</sup>).
Rearranging and integrating for velocity v(x) with the boundary condition v = 0 at x = R yields v(x) = (P / 4&eta;l) (R<sup>2</sup> - x<sup>2</sup>).
To find the total volume rate of flow Q, integrate the discharge through elementary annular rings of area 2&pi;x dx from x = 0 to x = R: Q = &int; v(x) (2&pi;x dx).

derivations.title: Capillary Tubes in Series and Parallel
derivations.conditions: Two tubes of lengths l_1, l_2 and radii r_1, r_2 connected end-to-end (series) or side-by-side (parallel).
steps: For series combination, rate of flow Q is identical through both tubes: Q = \frac{\pi P_1 r_1^4}{8 \eta l_1} = \frac{\pi P_2 r_2^4}{8 \eta l_2}.
Total pressure drop P = P_1 + P_2 = Q \left(\frac{8 \eta l_1}{\pi r_1^4} + \frac{8 \eta l_2}{\pi r_2^4}\right).
Define hydrodynamic resistance R_v = \frac{8 \eta l}{\pi r^4}. Thus, P = Q (R_1 + R_2).
For parallel combination, total flow Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = P \left(\frac{\pi r_1^4}{8 \eta l_1} + \frac{\pi r_2^4}{8 \eta l_2}\right).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Distribution Across Capillary Radius
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic profile symmetric about the central axis, showing zero velocity at the walls (r = R) and maximum velocity at the center (r = 0).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that velocity gradient (dv/dr) is zero at the center and maximum at the inner wall, confirming non-uniform shear stress.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT multiple-choice questions regarding the nature of velocity profile in viscous flow.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rate of Flow (Q) versus Radius (r) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A non-linear steep curve representing a power-law relationship, plotting Q on the y-axis and r on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms that volume flow rate scales steeply with the fourth power of the radius (Q proportional to r<sup>4</sup>).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual interpretation where radius is doubled and the resulting change in flow rate must be calculated.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Poiseuille's Constant Head Viscometer Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing a constant head tank, capillary tube horizontal mount, measuring flask, and a thermometer.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the coefficient of viscosity (&eta;) of a liquid by measuring volume collected per unit time under a constant hydrostatic pressure head.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Practical physics viva and conceptual numericals on laboratory determination of viscosity.

solved_numericals.question: A capillary tube of radius 0.1 cm and length 10 cm is used to flow water under a constant pressure head of 20 cm of water. Calculate the volume of water flowing per second. (Take coefficient of viscosity of water = 0.001 Pa s, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, density of water = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: r = 0.1 cm = 10<sup>-3</sup> m, l = 10 cm = 0.1 m, &eta; = 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa s.
Calculate pressure difference P = h&rho;g = 0.2 m * 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup> * 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> = 1960 N/m<sup>2</sup>.
Apply Poiseuille's formula: Q = (\pi P r<sup>4</sup>) / (8 &eta; l).

solved_numericals.question: Two capillary tubes of same length and radii r and 2r are connected in series. If the total pressure difference across the combination is P, find the pressure difference across the second tube (radius 2r).
solution_steps: Viscous resistance of first tube: R<sub>1</sub> = 8&eta;l / (&pi; r<sup>4</sup>).
Viscous resistance of second tube: R<sub>2</sub> = 8&eta;l / (&pi; (2r)<sup>4</sup>) = R<sub>1</sub> / 16.
In series, rate of flow Q is identical, so pressure drop is directly proportional to resistance: P<sub>2</sub> = Q * R<sub>2</sub> and P = Q * (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>).
Ratio P<sub>2</sub> / P = R<sub>2</sub> / (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) = (R<sub>1</sub> / 16) / (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>1</sub>/16) = (1/16) / (17/16) = 1/17.

solved_numericals.question: If the radius of a capillary tube is increased by 10% while keeping the pressure difference and length constant, find the percentage increase in the rate of liquid flow.
solution_steps: Poiseuille's relation gives Q proportional to r<sup>4</sup> when P, &eta;, and l are constant.
Given percentage change in radius &Delta;r / r = +10% = 0.1.

assumptions_and_limitations: The liquid is assumed to be Newtonian with a constant coefficient of viscosity unaffected by shear rate.
The flow must be strictly streamline and laminar (Reynolds number < 2000); turbulence invalidates Poiseuille's equation.
The inner walls of the tube are rigid, perfectly smooth, and cylindrical, with a zero slip condition at the boundary.
End effects, kinetic energy head loss at entry, and gravitational head variations across the cross-section are neglected in the elementary form.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Liquid velocity is uniform across the entire cross-section of the capillary tube.
common_misconceptions.correct: Velocity varies parabolically, being maximum at the center and zero at the walls.
common_misconceptions.why: Viscous drag creates a shear stress gradient from the stationary walls to the central axis.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Doubling the radius of a capillary tube doubles the rate of liquid flow.
common_misconceptions.correct: Doubling the radius increases the rate of flow by a factor of 2<sup>4</sup> = 16.
common_misconceptions.why: Poiseuille's law establishes a fourth-power dependence of volume flow rate on the radius (Q &prop; r<sup>4</sup>).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Capillary flow rate depends on the total mass of liquid in the reservoir.
common_misconceptions.correct: Flow rate depends only on the hydrostatic pressure difference (P = h&rho;g) between the ends of the tube.
common_misconceptions.why: The absolute height of the liquid column above the entry does not drive flow; only the pressure drop across length l matters.

quick_revision: Poiseuille's formula states Q = &pi;Pr<sup>4</sup> / 8&eta;l for laminar tube flow.
The volume flow rate is extremely sensitive to tube radius, scaling as r<sup>4</sup>.
Viscosity decreases with an increase in temperature for liquids, thereby increasing the rate of flow Q.
Hydrodynamic resistance in series adds algebraically: R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>.
Velocity profile across the capillary diameter is parabolic with peak velocity at the center.
